chapter_note.about: An uninformed search knows only the problem: the states, the moves, the goal test and the step costs. It has no sense of where the goal is. Every strategy is the same loop. Take a node off the frontier, test it, add its children. The frontier structure sets the strategy: a queue gives BFS, a stack gives DFS, and a priority queue gives uniform-cost search. chapter_note.simple: Search is how a program finds a path or an answer by trying options one after another. An uninformed search has no hint about where the goal is, so it tries options in a fixed pattern: nearest first (BFS), deepest first (DFS) or cheapest first (UCS). Each pattern is just a different way to keep the waiting list of places to try. Some patterns are safe but use a lot of memory. Others use almost none but can get lost. Iterative deepening and searching from both ends are tricks to get the best of both. In exam words: uninformed search, frontier structures, expansion order, UCS, DLS and IDS, completeness and optimality, time and space in b, d and m, and bidirectional search.

cards.title: Uninformed vs informed
cards.simple: Imagine finding the exit of a maze. A blind search knows only the walls and the moves, and it only learns where the exit is when it gets there. An informed search has a hint, like a friend shouting 'warmer, colder'. That hint is a guess of how far the exit still is. In search, an uninformed algorithm uses only the problem as it is given: the states, the moves, the goal test and the costs. An informed one also uses a guess called a heuristic. In exam words: uninformed (blind) search uses no h(n); informed (heuristic) search, such as greedy and A*, ranks nodes using h(n).
cards.idea: A search algorithm must pick which node to try next. An **uninformed** one picks using only what the problem states: the moves, the goal test and the costs so far. An **informed** one also uses a guess h(n) of how far each node is from the goal. So the test is one question. Does the ranking use h(n)?
cards.idea_full: Every search keeps a frontier, the list of nodes it has seen but not yet tried. The only difference between algorithms is how they choose the next node from it. BFS chooses the oldest. DFS chooses the newest. UCS chooses the one with the cheapest path so far. None of these needs to know where the goal is, so they are blind. Greedy and A* use an estimate h(n) of the cost still to go, so they lean toward the goal. That estimate is the heuristic. Cleverness is not the test: iterative deepening is clever but still uninformed.
cards.definition:
Uninformed (blind) search uses only the problem definition: states, actions, goal test and step costs. Examples: BFS, DFS, uniform-cost search (UCS), depth-limited search (DLS), iterative deepening (IDS) and bidirectional search.

Informed (heuristic) search also uses h(n), an estimate of the cheapest cost from node n to a goal. Examples: greedy best-first search, A* and IDA*.

The path cost g(n) is the cost already paid from the start to n. It is known exactly, so using it does not make a search informed.
cards.intuition_full: The word 'informed' is about information that the problem did not hand you for free. A map with road lengths tells you what each step costs, and that is part of the problem. A straight-line distance to the goal is a guess you add on top. That guess is h(n). Think of two taxi drivers in a new city. One follows fixed rules like 'try the nearest streets first' and has no sense of direction. The other glances at a compass pointing at the destination. The second driver is informed. The compass can be wrong, but it usually helps. That is why greedy and A* sit in one family, and BFS, DFS and UCS sit in another. UCS looks sophisticated because it uses costs, but costs are already in the problem. It still has no idea which way the goal lies.

example.setup: Sort these six into uninformed or informed by asking whether the frontier ranking uses h(n): BFS, DFS, bidirectional BFS, greedy best-first, A*, IDA*.
steps: Write down what each ranks by. BFS: depth. DFS: newest node. Bidirectional BFS: depth from each end. Greedy: h. A*: g + h. IDA*: g + h.
BFS, DFS and bidirectional BFS never use h. They are uninformed.
Greedy uses h, A* uses g + h and IDA* cuts off on g + h. All of them use h, so they are informed.
Result: BFS, DFS and bidirectional BFS are uninformed. Greedy, A* and IDA* are informed.
example.answer: Uninformed: BFS, DFS, bidirectional BFS. Informed: greedy, A*, IDA*.

examples.setup: Which statements are true? (i) UCS is informed because it uses step costs. (ii) Iterative deepening is uninformed. (iii) Greedy best-first search ranks by h(n) alone. (iv) A* run with h(n) = 0 for every node orders its frontier exactly like UCS.
steps: (i) UCS ranks by g(n), the cost already paid. g is part of the problem, not an estimate. So UCS is uninformed, and the statement is false.
(ii) IDS repeats depth-limited search and uses only depth. It uses no h. True.
(iii) Greedy ranks by h(n) and ignores g. True.
(iv) With h = 0 the A* key is f = g + 0 = g, which is the UCS key. True.
examples.answer: (ii), (iii) and (iv) are true. (i) is false. The trap avoided is calling UCS informed just because it 'uses costs'.

examples.answer: No. The table is a distractor. Use h only when the algorithm is greedy, A* or IDA*.

cards.title: Frontier data structures
cards.simple: Think of a to-do list of places to explore. A queue is a line at a shop: the person who arrived first is served first. A stack is a pile of plates: you grab the plate you put down last. BFS uses a line, so it finishes all the nearby places before going further. DFS uses a pile, so it keeps diving down the newest path before it comes back. UCS uses a list that always serves the cheapest place first. In exam words: BFS uses a FIFO queue, DFS a LIFO stack, and UCS a priority queue ordered by g(n).
cards.idea: The **frontier** is the list of nodes found but not yet expanded. Every uninformed search is the same loop: remove one node, test it, add its children. Only the data structure changes. BFS uses a **queue** (first in, first out). DFS uses a **stack** (last in, first out). UCS uses a **priority queue** ordered by the cost so far.
cards.idea_full: Here is the loop. Take a node off the frontier. If it is the goal, stop. Otherwise add its children to the frontier. Repeat. A queue hands out the oldest node, so the search spreads out level by level. A stack hands out the newest node, so the search dives down one branch to the bottom before backing up. A priority queue hands out the node with the smallest g(n). There is one catch with a stack. The last child pushed is the first one popped, so a stack reverses the order of the children.
cards.definition:
Frontier loop: remove a node from the frontier, goal-test it, add its children.

BFS: FIFO queue. Remove from the front, add at the back.
DFS: LIFO stack. Remove from the top, add on top.
UCS: priority queue. Remove the node with the smallest g(n), the cost of the path so far.

Peak frontier size is the memory cost. BFS holds about b^d nodes and DFS only about b·m. Here b is the branching factor, d the depth of the goal and m the maximum depth.
cards.intuition_full: A frontier is a waiting room, and the data structure decides who is called next. In a queue, the node that has waited longest goes first. Everything at depth 1 is called before anything at depth 2, so BFS visits level by level. In a stack, the newest arrival goes first. After a node is expanded its children arrive last, so they go first, and the search plunges down. That is also why a stack holds so few nodes. It keeps one path and a few waiting siblings, while a queue must hold a whole level. A priority queue is a queue where a cheaper g(n) jumps ahead. Be careful with the stack. If you push A, B, C in that order, C pops first. To have A expanded first, push C, B, A. A question that says 'expands the alphabetically first child first' means exactly this.

example.setup: Tree: S has children A and B. A has children C and D. B has the child E. Children are taken in alphabetical order. Show the BFS queue and the DFS stack, and the order in which each expands.
steps: Both frontiers start with S. BFS removes from the front of its queue. DFS removes from the top of its stack.
Expand S. BFS adds A then B at the back: [A, B]. DFS pushes B first, then A, so A is on top: [B, A].
Expand A. The BFS queue becomes [B, C, D]. DFS pops A and pushes D then C: [B, D, C], with C on top.
BFS expands B and adds E: [C, D, E]. DFS pops C. It is a leaf, so nothing is added: [B, D].
BFS expands C: [D, E]. DFS pops D: [B].
BFS expands D: [E]. DFS pops B and pushes E: [E].
Both expand E last. BFS order: S, A, B, C, D, E. DFS order: S, A, C, D, B, E.
example.answer: BFS order S, A, B, C, D, E (level by level). DFS order S, A, C, D, B, E (it dives first).

examples.setup: A complete binary tree has depth 4, so it has 31 nodes. The goal is the last leaf, so the search must go through everything before it. The goal test happens on removal. The frontier size is measured after each expansion. What is the peak frontier size for BFS and for DFS (DFS pushes both children and expands the left one first)?
steps: BFS finishes one level before it starts the next, so the frontier is biggest when it holds a whole level of fresh children.
Just after BFS expands the last node at depth 3, the frontier holds all 16 nodes at depth 4. The BFS peak is 16.
DFS keeps one path plus the right-hand sibling that is still waiting at each level.
Going down the left side: after expanding the root the frontier has 2 nodes. Each deeper expansion removes 1 and adds 2, so the frontier grows by 1.
After expanding the left node at depth 3: the waiting right siblings at depths 1, 2 and 3 (3 nodes) plus its 2 children is 5.
Later pops never exceed that, so the DFS peak is 5. The formula (b - 1) × m + 1 = 1 × 4 + 1 = 5 agrees.
examples.answer: BFS peak 16, DFS peak 5. BFS memory grows like b^d and DFS memory like b·m.

examples.setup: S has three children A, B and C. DFS pushes them on the stack in alphabetical order. Which child is expanded first, and how do you get A first?
steps: Expand S. Push A, then B, then C. The stack from bottom to top is [A, B, C].
DFS removes from the top, so the first child expanded is C, not A.
To expand A first, push the children in reverse order: C, then B, then A. The stack is [C, B, A], with A on top.
Many questions say 'DFS expands the alphabetically first child first'. Treat that as the removal order, and push in reverse to match it.
examples.answer: Pushing alphabetically expands C first. To expand A first, push C, B, A.

cards.title: Expansion order, ties, graph vs tree search
cards.simple: To trace a search by hand, write down three rules before you start. First, which child goes first when there is a tie, usually alphabetical order. Second, when to stop: you stop when the goal is taken off the waiting list, not the moment you first spot it. Third, whether you remember where you have already been. If you do, you never revisit a place, which also stops you walking in circles. Then you just follow the list, step by step. In exam words: fix the tie-break, test the goal on removal, and keep an explored set in graph search.
cards.idea: To trace a search by hand, fix three rules first. Take children in the stated order. Test the goal when a node is **removed** from the frontier, not when it is generated. In graph search keep an **explored set** so no node is expanded twice. Then write the frontier after every step.
cards.idea_full: Search questions are bookkeeping, and most lost marks are rule slips. A tie-break such as 'alphabetical' says which child is generated first, and for a queue that is also the order they leave. The goal test on removal matters most for UCS and A*, where a goal can be generated early with a bad cost and a better path may arrive later. An explored set stops a node being expanded twice, and that also stops DFS going round a cycle. A node already waiting in the frontier is usually not added again. Follow the exact convention in the question.
cards.definition:
Conventions to fix before tracing:
1. Order: which child is taken first (alphabetical, or ascending number).
2. Goal test: when the node is removed from the frontier.
3. Repeats: graph search keeps an explored set, and skips nodes already in the frontier. Tree search does not.

If the question gives its own rule, such as 'always expand the smallest-numbered state', that rule replaces FIFO and LIFO.
cards.intuition_full: Think of a trace table in programming. You do not need cleverness, only discipline. Write the frontier, remove one node, write what you added, and note what you skipped. The explored set is your memory. Without it, a graph with a cycle sends the search round in circles, because an undirected edge lets you walk straight back to the parent. The removal test is about honesty. Generating the goal only means 'I can see it from here'. Removal means 'it is the best thing waiting, and I am taking it now'. For BFS the result is usually the same, but for UCS and A* testing early gives the wrong, costlier path. And if the question defines its own picking rule, trust it over the textbook. The textbook structure only matters when the question lets it decide.

example.setup: Undirected graph with edges S-A, S-B, A-C, B-C, C-G. Start S, goal G. Run BFS as graph search with children in alphabetical order. Give the expansion order.
steps: The frontier is [S] and the explored set is empty. Children go in alphabetical order.
Remove S and expand it. Add A and B. Explored: S.
Remove A. Its neighbours are S (explored) and C (new). Add C. The frontier is [B, C].
Remove B. Its neighbours are S (explored) and C (already waiting). Skip both. The frontier is [C].
Remove C. A and B are explored. G is new, so add it. The frontier is [G].
Remove G. It is the goal, so stop. Expanded: S, A, B, C. The path is S, A, C, G.
example.answer: S, A, B and C are expanded. Then G is removed and passes the goal test. The path is S, A, C, G.

examples.setup: Undirected graph with edges S-A, S-B, A-C, B-C, C-G. Start S, goal G. Run BFS as graph search with children in alphabetical order. Give the expansion order.

A state that is already generated is not added again. Both BFS and DFS are defined by one rule: always expand the smallest-numbered unexpanded state. cards.title: Uniform-cost search
cards.simple: Imagine paying a fee for every road you take, and you always continue from the place where you have spent the least so far. That is uniform-cost search. If you later find a cheaper way to a place already on your list, you cross out the old price and write the new one. And you only declare victory when the goal is the cheapest thing on your list, not the first time you see it. In exam words: UCS expands the node with the lowest path cost g(n), replaces a frontier entry by a cheaper path, tests the goal on removal, and is optimal for positive step costs.
cards.idea: **Uniform-cost search** always expands the frontier node with the smallest path cost so far, g(n). If a cheaper path to a frontier node turns up, it **replaces** the old entry. Stop when the goal is **removed**, not when it is first generated. With positive step costs, the first goal removed is a cheapest one.
cards.idea_full: BFS counts steps. UCS counts money. Keep the frontier sorted by g, the total cost from the start. Each time, take the cheapest node. Its neighbours get the cost g plus the edge cost. If a neighbour is already waiting with a higher cost, replace it. When the goal finally sits at the front, every other waiting node costs at least as much. So no cheaper path can appear later, provided every step costs something positive. That is why UCS is optimal, and why testing the goal early would be wrong.
cards.definition:
$$g(n)=g(\text{parent})+c(\text{parent},n)$$

Symbols: g(n) is the cost of the path from the start to n. c(parent, n) is the cost of the single edge into n. The frontier is a priority queue keyed on g. UCS is complete and optimal if every step cost is at least some small number ε > 0. With h(n) = 0 for all n, A* is exactly UCS.
cards.intuition_full: Think of a flood spreading from the start, but not at an equal speed: each road takes as long as its cost. UCS is that flood. The first time it reaches the goal, it has arrived by the fastest road, because all the slower floods are still behind. That is also why generating the goal is not enough. A goal can be reached early along an expensive road while a cheap road is still waiting in the queue. UCS needs positive costs, since a zero-cost loop could keep the flood spinning without moving forward. In effect this is Dijkstra's algorithm, which stops as soon as the target is settled.

example.setup: Weighted graph: S to A costs 1, S to B costs 4, A to G costs 8, B to G costs 3. Run UCS from S to G.
steps: The frontier is [S:0]. UCS orders it by g, the cost so far.
Remove S. Add A with g = 1 and B with g = 4. The frontier is [A:1, B:4].
Remove A (g = 1). G is reached with g = 1 + 8 = 9. Add G:9. Do not stop yet, because G is only generated.
Remove B (g = 4). G via B costs 4 + 3 = 7, which beats 9. Replace the old entry. The frontier is [G:7].
Remove G. The goal test passes with cost 7 along S, B, G.
example.answer: Cost 7 along S, B, G. The expansion order is S, A, B, and then G is removed.

cards.title: Depth-limited and iterative deepening
cards.simple: Imagine searching a huge building for a lost phone. Depth-limited search says 'I will go at most 3 floors down, no further'. If the phone is on floor 5, you miss it. Iterative deepening fixes this by repeating: first look 0 floors down, then 1, then 2, and so on until you find it. It re-searches the top floors every round, which sounds wasteful, but the lowest floors are so much bigger that the repeats hardly matter. It also finds the shallowest phone, and it only needs to remember one path. In exam words: IDS runs depth-limited DFS with limits 0, 1, 2, and so on. It is complete and finds a shallowest goal, with time O(b^d) and space O(bd).
cards.idea: **Depth-limited search** (DLS) is DFS that refuses to go below depth ℓ. It answers **cutoff** if the limit stopped it. **Iterative deepening** (IDS) runs DLS with ℓ = 0, 1, 2, ... until it finds a goal. So it finds a **shallowest** goal like BFS, but keeps only one path in memory like DFS. The shallow nodes are visited again in every round.
cards.idea_full: DFS is cheap in memory but can dive forever. BFS is safe but needs a lot of memory. IDS takes the good part of each. A depth limit stops the dive. Raising the limit one step at a time means the first goal found is at the lowest limit that works, which is the shallowest depth. Each round starts again from the root, so the root is visited in every round. That repeated work is small because a tree is bottom-heavy: the last level is bigger than all the others added together.
cards.definition:
DLS(ℓ): run DFS but treat nodes at depth ℓ as leaves. The result is a goal path, **cutoff** (the limit blocked some node), or **failure** (nothing is left to try).

IDS: for ℓ = 0, 1, 2, ... run DLS(ℓ) and stop when the result is not cutoff.

$$\text{nodes generated by IDS}=\sum_{j=0}^{d}(d-j+1)\,b^{j}$$

Symbols: b is the branching factor, d is the depth of the shallowest goal, and j is a level. A node at level j is generated in every round whose limit is at least j. That is d − j + 1 rounds. IDS time is O(b^d) and space is O(bd). It is optimal when every step costs the same.
cards.intuition_full: Why is repeating cheap? In a tree with b = 10, level 5 has 100,000 nodes and level 4 has only 10,000. Redoing everything above the last level costs about a tenth extra. The deeper the goal, the more the last level dominates. So IDS pays a small tax and gets BFS's guarantee of a shallowest goal. The memory saving is large: DFS stores only the current path, about b·d nodes, while BFS stores a whole level. DLS alone has two catches. If ℓ is too small, it returns cutoff. That means 'not found within this limit', not 'no solution'. If ℓ is larger than needed, it may return a deeper goal and miss a shallower one. IDS fixes both by raising the limit slowly. When counting visits, count the root once for every round.

Total visits: 1 + 3 + 4 = 8. The root S was visited in all 3 rounds.
The path is S, A, D. It is a shallowest goal.

cards.title: Completeness and optimality
cards.simple: Ask two questions about any search method. Will it always find a solution if one exists? That is called complete. And will the first solution it finds be the cheapest? That is called optimal. BFS checks the nearest places first, so it finds the closest goal, which is the cheapest only if every step costs the same. DFS can get lost down a never-ending road, so it may never come back, and it may find a long route first. UCS always follows the cheapest road so far, so it finds the cheapest route even when roads cost different amounts. In exam words: BFS is complete and optimal for equal step costs; DFS is neither; UCS is complete and optimal if step costs are at least a small positive ε; IDS behaves like BFS.
cards.idea: Two questions rate a search. **Complete**: does it find a solution whenever one exists? **Optimal**: is the first solution it returns a cheapest one? BFS is complete, and optimal when every step costs the same. DFS is neither. UCS is both when every step costs at least a small positive amount. IDS behaves like BFS.
cards.idea_full: BFS is complete because it reaches every depth in turn, so a goal at a finite depth is eventually found (b must be finite). It returns the shallowest goal. That is the cheapest only if all steps cost the same, since then fewer steps means lower cost. With unequal costs a longer path can be cheaper. DFS can fall into a cycle or an infinite branch and never come back, and it returns the first goal it meets, which may be deep and expensive. UCS looks at paths in order of cost, so it is optimal for any positive costs. IDS repeats DLS, so it inherits BFS's properties.
cards.definition:
Complete: finds a solution if one exists.
Optimal: returns a least-cost solution.

With b finite and goal depth d:
BFS: complete. Optimal if all step costs are equal.
DFS: not complete (cycles, infinite depth). Not optimal.
UCS: complete and optimal if every step cost is at least ε > 0.
DLS: not complete if ℓ < d. Not optimal.

cards.intuition_full: Picture three explorers sent to find the cheapest route out of a building. The first (BFS) checks all the nearby rooms before going deeper, so the first exit found is the closest one. 'Closest' means fewest doors, and that equals cheapest only if every door costs the same. The second (DFS) always runs down the newest corridor. If a corridor loops or goes on for ever, he is stuck for good. And the first exit he finds may be at the end of a long route. The third (UCS) keeps the bill for every path and always extends the cheapest bill. A cheap-looking first step cannot fool him, because he compares total bills. The 'at least ε' condition matters. If some steps cost 0, you can loop for free forever, and the bill never grows. IDS is BFS in disguise, so it has the same strengths and the same weakness.

cards.title: Time and space in b, d, m
cards.simple: Picture a family tree where every person has b children. Level 0 has 1 person, level 1 has b, level 2 has b times b, and each level is b times bigger than the one before. BFS has to remember a whole level, which is huge. DFS only remembers one line of ancestors and the brothers and sisters still waiting, which is tiny, but it might wander down a very deep line and take forever. Iterative deepening mixes the two: a BFS-style answer with DFS-size memory. In exam words: BFS has time and space O(b^d); DFS has time O(b^m) and space O(bm); IDS has time O(b^d) and space O(bd). Here b is the branching factor, d the goal depth and m the maximum depth.
cards.idea: Three numbers describe a search tree: **b** (children per node), **d** (depth of the shallowest goal) and **m** (maximum depth). A level at depth k has about b^k nodes. BFS time and space are both **O(b^d)**. DFS time is **O(b^m)** but its space is only **O(bm)**. IDS has BFS-like time O(b^d) and DFS-like space O(bd).
cards.idea_full: Counting nodes is the whole story. Level k has b^k nodes. A search that must look at every node down to depth d does about b^d work, because the last level swamps all the rest. BFS also has to keep that last level in memory, so its space is b^d too. DFS stores only the current path plus the siblings still waiting, which is about b·m nodes. But DFS may go down to depth m before it finds anything, so its worst-case time is b^m, and m can be much bigger than d. IDS runs DFS in rounds, so its memory is b·d, and its time is still b^d up to a small factor.
cards.definition:
$$\text{BFS: } O(b^{d})\text{ time and space}\qquad \text{DFS: } O(b^{m})\text{ time},\ O(bm)\text{ space}\qquad \text{IDS: } O(b^{d})\text{ time},\ O(bd)\text{ space}$$

Symbols: b is the branching factor, d the depth of the shallowest goal, m the maximum depth of the tree. The number of nodes down to depth d is $1+b+b^2+\dots+b^d=\dfrac{b^{d+1}-1}{b-1}$, which is about $b^d$ when b is at least 2.
cards.intuition_full: Why does the last level dominate? Because each level is b times bigger than the one before. With b = 4 and d = 3 the levels are 1, 4, 16, 64. The last level, 64, is three-quarters of the total 85. This is a geometric series, and its largest term controls the sum. For DFS, think of a hiker with a trail log. The hiker remembers the current trail (depth m) and, at each fork on it, the other branches still to try. Each of the m forks has b − 1 other branches, so the hiker holds (b − 1)·m + 1 nodes, which is O(bm). That is why DFS memory is so small. But the hiker may walk down a trail 20 forks deep before finding anything, which costs b^m time. Space O(bm) and time O(b^m) look alike on the page and differ hugely in size.

example.setup: A tree has b = 4. The shallowest goal is at depth d = 3 and the maximum depth is m = 3. Count the nodes on each level, and the most nodes that BFS and DFS ever hold.
steps: Level k has 4^k nodes: 1, 4, 16, 64.
All the nodes down to depth 3: 1 + 4 + 16 + 64 = 85. The formula agrees: (4^4 − 1) / (4 − 1) = (256 − 1) / 3 = 85. The last level is 64 of the 85.
BFS memory: it holds a whole level, up to 64 nodes (4^3).
DFS memory: one path plus the waiting siblings. (b − 1)·m + 1 = 3 × 3 + 1 = 10 nodes.
example.answer: 85 nodes in total. BFS holds up to 64 at once and DFS at most 10.

123,456 against 111,111 is only about 11% more.

cards.title: Bidirectional search
cards.simple: Two friends looking for each other in a big park do better if both walk toward the middle than if one of them searches the whole park. Bidirectional search runs two searches at once, one from the start and one backward from the goal, and it stops when they meet. Each only goes half the distance. Because the number of places to check grows so fast with distance, halving the distance saves a huge amount. The catch is that you must know exactly where the goal is, and you must be able to walk the roads backward. In exam words: bidirectional search runs two BFSs and meets in the middle, with time and space O(b^(d/2)). It needs predecessors and a single known goal.
cards.idea: **Bidirectional search** runs one search forward from the start and one backward from the goal, and stops when the two frontiers meet. Each side only goes about half the depth, d/2. That cuts time and space from O(b^d) to **O(b^(d/2))** per side. It needs a **known goal** and a way to step **backward** (predecessors).
cards.idea_full: A search tree grows huge with depth. Searching to depth d costs about b^d. Two searches of depth d/2 cost about 2·b^(d/2) together. For b = 10 and d = 6 that is 2,000 nodes instead of a million. The two searches must find a shared node, so each new node is checked against the other side's frontier. The path is the forward half joined to the backward half. For this you need the goal to be one named state, and the actions to be reversible so that you can find predecessors.
cards.definition:
$$\text{time and space: } O\!\left(b^{d/2}\right)\text{ per direction, about } 2\,b^{d/2}\text{ in total}$$

Symbols: b is the branching factor and d is the depth of the shallowest solution. Each side searches to depth d/2. Requirements: (1) an explicit goal state, (2) a predecessor function so the backward search can step toward the start, (3) a check that detects when a node is in both frontiers.
cards.intuition_full: Think of the nodes within distance r of a point as a circle that grows with r. In a tree, the number of nodes within distance r grows like b^r. A single search must grow its circle to radius d. Two searches grow their circles to only d/2 each, and then they touch. Because of the exponent, the saving is not 'half'. It is a square root, since b^(d/2) is the square root of b^d. A million nodes become a thousand. That is the whole appeal. The price is in the preconditions. If the goal is 'any checkmate position', there is no single place to start the backward search. If moves cannot be undone easily, you cannot compute predecessors. And you must store at least one side's frontier to test for a meeting, which is why space stays as large as b^(d/2).

example.setup: Graph with two routes: S-A-C-E-G and S-B-D-F-G, all edges cost 1. Run bidirectional BFS from S and from G, one round at a time, and compare with one-way BFS.
steps: The forward frontier is {S}. The backward frontier is {G}.
Round 1: forward expands S and reaches A and B. Backward expands G and reaches E and F.
Round 2: forward expands A and B and reaches C and D.
Backward expands E and F and reaches C and D. These are already in the forward frontier, so the frontiers meet.
Join the halves: S, A, C, E, G (or the lower route). Each side went down 2 levels.
Expansions: 3 forward (S, A, B) plus 3 backward (G, E, F) is 6, against 7 for one-way BFS (S, A, B, C, D, E, F).
example.answer: The searches meet at C and D after 6 expansions. One-way BFS needs 7. The gap is small only because the graph is tiny.

examples.setup: You want to find a route between two named cities on a road map, and you also want to solve a chess endgame by reaching any checkmate. For which one can bidirectional search be used?

Road map: the goal is one named city. Roads can be driven both ways, so predecessors are easy. The method works.
Chess: there are a huge number of different checkmate positions. The backward search would have to start from all of them, and listing the moves that lead into a position is hard.
So it fits the route problem, not 'reach any checkmate'.
examples.answer: Use it for the road route. It does not fit the checkmate goal, because there is no single goal state and the moves are hard to reverse.

After each expansion, check whether a new node is in the other frontier.

It is optimal only if both searches are BFS with equal step costs and the meeting rule is checked carefully.
Space is the weak point: one side's frontier must be stored for the intersection test.

$$\text{time and space: } O\!\left(b^{d/2}\right)\text{ per direction, about } 2\,b^{d/2}\text{ in total}$$

Symbols: b is the branching factor and d is the depth of the shallowest solution. Each side searches to depth d/2. Requirements: (1) an explicit goal state, (2) a predecessor function so the backward search can step toward the start, (3) a check that detects when a node is in both frontiers.

**Worked example.** Graph with two routes: S-A-C-E-G and S-B-D-F-G, all edges cost 1. Run bidirectional BFS from S and from G, one round at a time, and compare with one-way BFS.

1. The forward frontier is {S}. The backward frontier is {G}.
2. Round 1: forward expands S and reaches A and B. Backward expands G and reaches E and F.
3. Round 2: forward expands A and B and reaches C and D.
4. Backward expands E and F and reaches C and D. These are already in the forward frontier, so the frontiers meet.
5. Join the halves: S, A, C, E, G (or the lower route). Each side went down 2 levels.
6. Expansions: 3 forward (S, A, B) plus 3 backward (G, E, F) is 6, against 7 for one-way BFS (S, A, B, C, D, E, F).

**Answer:** The searches meet at C and D after 6 expansions. One-way BFS needs 7. The gap is small only because the graph is tiny.

**Check yourself:** b = 10 and d = 6. Roughly how many nodes does bidirectional BFS generate?

*Answer:* About 2 × 10^3 = 2,000, against about 10^6 for one-way BFS.
cards.trap: Using it when the goal is not a single known state, or when you cannot step backward. A second slip is calling O(b^(d/2)) 'half the work'. It is the square root of the work, a far bigger saving, but the memory is still large.

It shows that halving the depth halves the exponent. In GATE: you compare complexities, and you state when bidirectional search can or cannot be used.

scenes.title: Sorting algorithms by what they rank by

steps.caption: Six algorithms. Each box shows what it ranks its frontier by. One question sorts them: does the ranking use a heuristic h(n)?
BFS ranks by depth, DFS by recency, bidirectional BFS by depth from each end. None of them uses h. They go under Uninformed.
Greedy ranks by h. A* ranks by g + h. IDA* cuts off on g + h. All three use h, so they are Informed.
Result: BFS, DFS and bidirectional are uninformed. Greedy, A* and IDA* are informed. Costs already in the problem are not a heuristic.

scenes.title: BFS vs DFS: frontier contents each step

steps.caption: Both algorithms start with the root S on the frontier. Watch where each one removes from.
Expand S. BFS adds A, B at the back. DFS pushes B then A, so A sits on top.
Expand A. BFS takes it from the front and queues C, D behind B. DFS takes it from the top and pushes C on top, so it heads down.
BFS expands B (same depth as A). DFS expands C, a leaf, and backs up to D.
BFS reaches C only now. DFS has already finished A's subtree with D.

set.text: BFS order: S A B C
DFS order: S A C D

steps.caption: BFS finishes depth 2 with D. DFS finally goes back to B and pushes E.

set.text: BFS order: S A B C D
DFS order: S A C D B

steps.caption: Same nodes, different order. BFS goes level by level; DFS dives, so its stack stays short.

set.text: BFS order: S A B C D E
DFS order: S A C D B E

scenes.title: Expansion order with an explored set

steps.caption: Graph search with a queue (BFS). Children are taken in alphabetical order. The frontier starts as [S]. Nothing is explored yet.
Remove S and expand it. Add its children A and B. Explored: S.
Remove A. Its neighbours are S (already explored, skip) and C (new). Add C. Frontier [B, C].
Remove B. Its neighbours are S (explored) and C (already in the frontier). Skip both. Frontier [C].
Remove C. A and B are explored. G is new, so add it. Frontier [G].
Remove G and test it: it is the goal, so stop. Four nodes were expanded (S, A, B, C) and the path is S, A, C, G.

scenes.title: UCS: cheaper path replaces a frontier entry

objects.label: Priority queue (lowest g on the left)

steps.caption: UCS keeps the frontier sorted by g, the cost so far. Start with S at cost 0.
Remove S. Add A at 1 and B at 4. The queue stays sorted by g.
Remove A. G is reached with g = 1 + 8 = 9. Do not stop: G is only generated, not removed.
Remove B. G via B costs 4 + 3 = 7, cheaper than 9, so the old G entry is replaced.
G is now at the front. Removing it passes the goal test with cost 7, the cheapest path S, B, G.

set.text: goal removed: cost 7 via S, B, G

steps.caption: Goal is D at depth 2. Pass 1 uses limit 0, so DLS can only look at the root. It returns cutoff.
Pass 2: limit 1. It restarts at the root, so S is visited again, then A and B. Still no goal.
Pass 3: limit 2. DFS order is S, A, C, D. The goal D is found at depth 2, a shallowest goal.
Total visits 1 + 3 + 4 = 8. The root was visited in all 3 passes. The repeats are cheap because the last level dominates.

scenes.title: Complete and optimal: BFS, DFS, UCS, IDS

objects.text: b finite, step costs at least e > 0, cycles allowed

steps.caption: The assumptions: finite branching factor b, step costs at least a small positive e, and a state space that may have cycles or unbounded depth.
BFS finds the shallowest goal and always finds one. That is the cheapest goal only when every step costs the same.
DFS can dive into a cycle or an infinite branch and never return, so it is not complete. It may also reach a deep, costly goal first, so it is not optimal.
UCS expands by cost so far. With costs of at least e it always finishes and returns the cheapest path, equal costs or not.
IDS behaves like BFS: complete, and optimal only when all steps cost the same. It returns a shallowest goal, not a cheapest one.
Only UCS stays optimal when step costs differ. DFS is neither complete nor optimal.

scenes.title: Nodes per level and memory: BFS against DFS

steps.caption: A tree where every node has b = 4 children. Level d has 4 to the power d nodes: 1, 4, 16, 64.
Add them to find all nodes down to depth 3: 1 + 4 + 16 + 64 = 85. The last level alone is 64 of the 85, so the total is about b to the power d.
BFS time is O(b^d). BFS memory is also O(b^d): it keeps a whole level in the frontier, up to 64 nodes.
DFS keeps one path and the unexpanded siblings on it: (b - 1) x m + 1 = 3 x 3 + 1 = 10 nodes. That is O(bm), tiny next to 64.

set.text: BFS keeps up to 64, DFS only 10

scenes.title: Bidirectional search meets in the middle

steps.caption: Two searches at once. One goes forward from the start S. The other goes backward from the goal G. Each is a BFS.
Round 1. Forward expands S and reaches A and B. Backward expands G and reaches E and F.
Round 2. Forward expands A and B and reaches C and D.
Backward expands E and F. They reach C and D, which the forward side already holds. The two frontiers meet.
Join the halves: S, A, C, E, G (or S, B, D, F, G). Each side only went down 2 levels, half of the 4.
Count: 3 expansions forward plus 3 backward is 6, against 7 for one-way BFS. The tree is tiny, so the saving is small. For b = 10 and d = 6 it is about 2 x 10^3 against 10^6.
